stories.head: Pope Leo needs no further cancer treatment, doctors say
stories.say: Pope Leo's doctors say he needs no further cancer treatment. Tests after his surgery last week confirmed the tumour in his right lung had not spread.
stories.stand: Final tests after surgery on his right lung confirmed the cancer was localised, the pontiff's physician and surgeon said in a statement.
body: Pope Leo XIV will not need further treatment after surgery for lung cancer, his doctors said on Wednesday. The statement came from his physician, Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora.

They said final tests confirmed the tumour was a lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, and that the disease was localised. An oncology assessment found no further therapy was needed.

Surgeons removed the tumour from his right lung on 13 October at Rome's Gemelli hospital. Dr Margaritora has said the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal exams, and the pope had no symptoms.
The pope has since resumed public appearances. He still plans to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November.

stories.head: US orders staff out of Saudi Arabia as airport attack kills one
stories.say: America has told non-emergency diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks. Separately, a strike on an airport in Dammam killed one person.
stories.stand: The State Department cited rising Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and infrastructure; one person was killed and eight hurt at an airport in Dammam.
body: The US State Department has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia. Spokesman Tommy Pigott said Yemen's Houthis had increasingly engaged in hostilities against the kingdom.
The department cited attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. Mr Pigott said the order applied only to Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said one person was killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, according to Al Jazeera. Separately, debris from a drone aimed at the Shaybah oilfield killed two people.
On 10 October, a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300.

stories.head: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume peace talks
stories.say: Russia says it is ready in principle to restart three-way peace talks with Ukraine and America next month. Overnight, missiles struck Kyiv, injuring six people, the mayor said.
stories.stand: Moscow said it would return to talks with Kyiv and Washington after the US midterms, as Zelensky backed freezing the front line.
body: Russia says it is ready in principle to resume three-way talks with Ukraine and the United States. The Kremlin made the offer after Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
Reports say the talks could take place in mid-November, after the US midterm elections. The Kremlin called recent Ukrainian and European proposals vague and lacking substance.
Volodymyr Zelensky said freezing the current front line was the most realistic first step towards a ceasefire. He said Ukraine must be directly involved in any talks and needs security guarantees.
Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight into Thursday. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said six people were injured. A drone attack on the city early on Wednesday killed two people.

stories.head: Russia frees jailed American teacher Stephen Hubbard
stories.say: Russia has freed Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher jailed on mercenary charges. Donald Trump says Vladimir Putin let him go at his request, with no swap.
stories.stand: The retired teacher, held for more than four years, was released as US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.
body: Russia has released Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher, during US envoy Steve Witkoff's talks with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday.

Russia accused Mr Hubbard of mercenary activity for Ukraine after capturing him there in 2022. He was sentenced in 2024 to almost seven years. His family maintain his innocence, and the US had declared him wrongfully detained.

Donald Trump said Mr Putin freed him at his request and that no swap was needed. Mr Trump later linked the release to his decision to waive new Russia sanctions, according to CBS News. Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin and called him a humanitarian.
He is the second American freed by Russia in about two months, after Robert Gilman in August. CBS reported he was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

stories.head: Macron hits back at foreign leaders as Paris bans protests
stories.say: Emmanuel Macron has called claims blaming immigration for France's riots stupid, accusing foreign leaders of exploiting them. Paris police have banned protests in central areas.
stories.stand: The French president rejected claims from abroad, including Trump's, blaming migrants for the riots, as police banned demonstrations near key Paris sites.
body: Emmanuel Macron has called claims blaming immigration for France's riots "unacceptable" and "stupid". Speaking in Qatar, he said foreign leaders were using the unrest for their own political campaigns.
Asked if he meant Donald Trump, he said "among others". Mr Trump had urged him to close France's borders. Mr Macron also said AI-generated images showed scenes that never happened in France.
Paris police banned gatherings in central areas from 8am to 8pm on Thursday. The ban covers sites including the Élysée Palace, both houses of parliament and the Champs-Élysées.
The unrest grew out of protests over the high cost of living, and thousands of people have been arrested. Night curfews were renewed on Wednesday in cities including Paris and Lyon.

stories.head: Macron secures Qatari gas as France and Qatar urge open Hormuz
stories.say: Emmanuel Macron says France has secured extra liquefied gas from Qatar for the winter. He and Qatar's emir also called for free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.stand: On his first state visit to Qatar, the French president announced an LNG supply deal and joined a call for free navigation in the Gulf.
body: Emmanuel Macron met Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, in Doha on Wednesday during his first state visit to Qatar.

Mr Macron said France had secured the equivalent of 2 terawatt-hours of liquefied natural gas a month for the winter. He said France also had commitments for 200,000 tonnes of diesel a month from the UAE and Bahrain.
In a joint statement, the two countries called for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz without constraints or fees. They also urged implementation of the Gaza ceasefire.
Mr Macron's Gulf tour included Saudi Arabia, where he made a surprise stop after Qatar to show support amid Houthi attacks.

stories.head: Kim Yo Jong says border loudspeakers will be ready within days
stories.say: North Korea's Kim Yo Jong says propaganda loudspeakers aimed at the South will be on standby along the border within days, and warns Seoul over warning shots.
stories.stand: The North Korean leader's sister said new countermeasures were on alert along the southern border, a day after announcing broadcasts would resume this month.
body: Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said on Thursday that anti-South Korea loudspeakers would be on standby along the border within days. Her statement was carried by state news agency KCNA.
She said new countermeasures would be put on alert along the entire southern border. A day earlier, she said loudspeaker broadcasts would resume by the end of October.
She accused South Korean troops of warning broadcasts and warning shots near the border. Seoul said the shots were legitimate and defensive.
South Korea halted its own broadcasts and dismantled its fixed border loudspeakers last year under President Lee Jae Myung.

stories.say: Israeli forces detained about ninety volunteers helping Palestinians pick olives near Bethlehem, among them US congressional nominee Brad Lander, who was later freed with a warning.
stories.stand: The volunteers were held after the army declared a West Bank grove a closed military zone; the military said the harvest was not coordinated.
body: Israeli forces detained about 90 volunteers helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives near Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday, according to Rabbis for Human Rights.
Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district, was among those held. He was released with a warning and said several others remained in detention.

The group said forces declared the area a closed military zone about two hours into the harvest, and held them although they agreed to leave. The Israeli military said the harvest was not coordinated in advance and posed a security risk.
The Jerusalem Post reported that authorities intended to deport the foreign activists.

stories.head: Mexico charges ex-prosecutor with treason over US role in drug raid
stories.say: A former state attorney general in Mexico has been charged with treason, accused of letting American agents take part in an anti-drug raid in Chihuahua in April.
stories.stand: César Jáuregui, former Chihuahua attorney general, is accused of allowing foreign agents into an operation; he has been held in pretrial detention.
body: César Jáuregui, the former attorney general of Chihuahua state, has been charged with treason. Federal prosecutors accuse him of allowing US agents to take part in an anti-drug operation in April.
Two US agents and two Mexican officials were killed in a car crash after the operation. Media reports identified the US agents as CIA members. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention.
President Claudia Sheinbaum has said her government did not know US agents were involved. Under Mexican law, foreign forces need federal approval to operate in the country.
Infobae reported the charge carries 5 to 40 years in prison. His lawyer says the evidence does not show he knew of the agents' involvement. A federal hearing resumes on Saturday.

stories.head: Albanese defends office's file on Helen Haines after attack
stories.say: Anthony Albanese has defended a document his office gave journalists about independent MP Helen Haines weeks before she was hit by a car, saying it was about policy, not personal.
stories.stand: The prime minister said the file listing the Indi MP's funding requests was not a personal attack; Haines lost both legs after Monday's alleged attack.
body: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has defended a document his office circulated to journalists about independent MP Helen Haines weeks before she was attacked, The Nightly reported.

The file listed funding requests by Ms Haines. It followed her questions about a $6 million grant to a golf club in Mr Albanese's electorate. He said on Thursday it showed "people of integrity stand up for their electorate".
Ms Haines was hit by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on Monday and has lost both legs. Her husband, Phil Haines, said she was stable.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged over the alleged attack, including intentionally causing serious injury, and remains in custody. Police allege it was targeted but say the motive is unknown.

stories.head: Venezuela talks end third round without an election date
stories.say: Venezuela's government and opposition have wrapped up a third round of talks in Caracas, agreeing to review laws used to bar candidates. But there's still no date for elections.
stories.stand: US-backed talks in Caracas produced pledges on political bans, courts and gold held in London, but left the election timetable unresolved.
body: Venezuela's government and opposition have ended a third round of US-backed talks in Caracas. The government delegation was led by Jorge Rodríguez and the opposition's by Dinorah Figuera.
Infobae reported that both sides agreed to review laws used to bar opposition figures from office. A joint commission will press the UK to return Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England.
El Tiempo reported progress towards renewing the Supreme Court. No date has been set for elections, and a new electoral council has not been appointed.
Opposition leader María Corina Machado has called protests for Thursday to demand an electoral timetable, El Tiempo said. Infobae said the next round is expected from 11 to 15 November.

stories.head: Teachers and students march in Athens over education funding
stories.say: Teachers, students and public-sector workers marched through Athens on Wednesday demanding more money for schools and universities. Police put the crowd at about ten thousand.
stories.stand: Police estimated about 10,000 marched in Athens as teachers' unions struck over pay, staffing and class sizes, with rallies in other Greek cities.
body: Students, teachers and public-sector workers marched from the University of Athens towards parliament on Wednesday. Police estimated about 10,000 people took part in Athens and its suburbs, Euronews reported.
Protesters demanded more funding for education, smaller classes, better facilities and affordable student housing. Rallies also took place in Thessaloniki, Patras and Crete.
The primary teachers' federation, DOE, called a 24-hour strike. It says nearly half of teachers earn no more than €1,000 a month and wants permanent appointments to vacant posts.
The Athens rally ended peacefully shortly before 2pm. Some banners were in French, in solidarity with protests in France.

stories.head: Killers who skip sentencing face cell confinement and visit bans
stories.say: Offenders who refuse to come to court for sentencing could be confined to their cells for three weeks and lose social visits, under rules the government has put before Parliament.
stories.stand: Judges in England and Wales will be able to impose prison punishments on offenders who refuse to attend their sentencing hearings, from next year.
body: Crown Court judges will gain powers to punish offenders who refuse to attend their sentencing, the Ministry of Justice said. The rules were laid before Parliament this week and are due to take effect next year.

Sanctions include up to 21 days of cellular confinement, loss of privileges for 84 days and loss of social visits for 27 days. Visits could then be limited to once every four weeks for 84 days. Visits from prisoners' children are exempt.

Offenders aged 18 to 20 in young offender institutions face shorter sanctions. The powers also cover offenders removed from court for disruptive behaviour. Refusing to attend can already bring a fine or up to two years' extra jail for contempt.

The government cited Thomas Cashman and Jordan McSweeney, who refused to hear their sentences. Prisons minister Catherine McKinnell said criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. The Prison Reform Trust questioned whether the sanctions would work.

stories.say: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated over an alleged rape inside the Houses of Parliament in 2016. The Met says no arrests have been made.
stories.stand: The Metropolitan Police is investigating a claim that the former DUP leader raped a woman inside Parliament in 2016; the inquiry is at an early stage.
body: The Metropolitan Police is investigating an allegation that a woman was raped inside the Houses of Parliament in 2016. The Met did not name the suspect, but described him as a 63-year-old man.
The suspect has been identified by outlets as Jeffrey Donaldson, the former DUP leader. The Police Service of Northern Ireland referred the report to the Met, which received it on 13 October.
The Met said the investigation was in its early stages, no arrests had been made and inquiries were ongoing. The woman is being supported by specialist officers.
Donaldson was jailed for 15 years this month for 18 historical sex offences against two women when they were children, committed between 1985 and 2008. His solicitor says an appeal has been lodged.

stories.head: Russell Brand accuser tells jury he treated her 'like an animal'
stories.say: The sixth woman to accuse Russell Brand told his trial she was raped at his London home in 2009, when she was 21. Brand, who is 51, denies all the charges against him.
stories.stand: The youngest of six women accusing the comedian told Southwark Crown Court she was raped at his home in 2009; Brand denies all charges.
body: The sixth woman to accuse Russell Brand has given evidence at his trial at Southwark Crown Court. She said he raped her at his London home in 2009, when she was 21.
In police interview videos played to the jury, she said she met him after a show at the Hammersmith Apollo. She said consensual sex at his home turned non-consensual and she begged him to stop.
She said that months later she told Brand by text that he had treated her like an animal, and that he apologised.
Brand, 51, denies three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault involving six women. His defence suggested she was an obsessed fan. The trial continues.

stories.head: MPs warn of 'glaring gaps' in UK defence of the High North
stories.say: MPs on the Defence Committee warn of glaring gaps in Britain's military strength in the High North, saying low submarine availability leaves cables and pipelines exposed to Russia.
stories.stand: The Commons Defence Committee says shortfalls in ships and submarines leave the UK, its nuclear deterrent and undersea cables vulnerable to Russia.
body: The Commons Defence Committee says the UK has glaring gaps in its military capability in the High North. It warns this leaves people, the nuclear deterrent and undersea cables and pipelines vulnerable to Russia.

The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, said submarine availability was shockingly low. It said the UK may have temporarily lost the ability to operate under Arctic ice. The Ministry of Defence has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap.

The Royal Navy has five Type 23 frigates and six Type 45 destroyers, against a requirement for 19. The committee wants none retired before eight Type 26 frigates arrive, and dramatic progress by 2030.
It also asked whether the Joint Expeditionary Force should focus more on the High North than the Baltic. The Ministry of Defence said it was clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.

body: Airbnb says hosts can no longer require guests to do tasks that take significant time or effort, or that a cleaner would normally do. Banned requests include stripping beds, washing dishes and taking out the bins.

stories.head: Two Jersey gas workers guilty of manslaughter over Haut du Mont blast
stories.say: Two gas workers have been convicted of manslaughter over the explosion that destroyed a block of flats in St Helier in 2022, killing ten people. Their employer was also found guilty.
stories.stand: A Jersey jury convicted two Island Energy workers over the 2022 explosion that killed ten people; it is still considering a third man's case.
body: Neil Armstrong, 58, and John Wright, 60, were found guilty of ten counts of gross negligence manslaughter. The charges relate to the Haut du Mont explosion in Jersey on 10 December 2022, which killed ten people.

Their employer, Jersey Gas, which trades as Island Energy, was convicted of two breaches of Jersey's health and safety at work law. The verdicts were unanimous, after 25 hours and eight minutes of deliberation.
The jury has not reached a verdict on a third worker, Lee Ward, 59, who denies the same charges. The judge has said a majority verdict can now be accepted.
ITV News reported that gas escaped from an open valve before the explosion, which brought down the block of flats.

body: Amin Belechguer, 29, of Clapham in south London, was jailed for four years at Maidstone Crown Court. He admitted dangerous driving offences committed between July 2024 and June 2025.

He was banned from driving and a deprivation order was made for his motorcycle. The judge said he arrogantly believed the rules of the road were not for him.

stories.say: Councils in England plan to resurface nearly seven thousand miles of road this year, the government says, as it releases another two hundred and twenty million pounds for repairs.
stories.stand: The Department for Transport released £220m in incentive funding and says resurfacing plans are more than 10% up on last year.
body: Councils in England expect to resurface nearly 7,000 miles of road in 2026 to 2027, the Department for Transport said. That is more than 10% up on the previous year.
The government released a further £220m of incentive-based funding for councils that meet performance targets. Later payments can be withheld from councils that fall short.
Councils project spending of £4.9bn on highway maintenance this year, up from £4.1bn in 2024 to 2025. The share of councils planning preventative repairs rose to 94% from 76%.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the figures showed the government was starting to turn a corner. The RAC said fixing roads was not an overnight job.

stories.head: UK house price growth slows to 0.9% as London values fall
stories.say: House price growth slowed for a fourth month running in August, to 0.9 per cent, with London prices falling. Private rents rose 3.8 per cent over the year to September.
stories.stand: The ONS says the average UK home cost £273,000 in August, while private rents rose 3.8% in the year to September.
body: UK house prices rose 0.9% in the year to August, down from 1.2% in July, the Office for National Statistics said. It was the fourth monthly slowdown in a row.
The average UK home cost £273,000. Prices rose 3.1% in Wales, 2.9% in Scotland and 0.4% in England. London prices fell 2.2%, driven by falling flat prices.
Average monthly private rent was £1,406 in September, up 3.8% on a year earlier. Scotland's rent growth of 0.7% was its lowest on record.

Richardson denies murder, the alternative charge of manslaughter and dangerous driving. The trial continues.

body: William Dunlop, known as Billy, began his fourth application for release at a Parole Board hearing on Wednesday, ITV News reported. He is now 63.

Dunlop strangled Julie Hogg, 22, in Billingham, County Durham, in 1989. Two earlier trials ended with hung juries. In 2006 he became the first person tried under the reformed double jeopardy rules, and was jailed for life.

Her son, Kevin Hogg, told the panel time had not eased his pain. Dunlop told the hearing he now understood the family's pain. ITV said three justice secretaries had previously overruled recommendations to move him to an open prison.
No decision has been announced.

stories.stand: The Justice Department wants an injunction lifted that halted border barrier work in and around Big Bend National Park in West Texas.
body: The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal with the US Supreme Court on Wednesday. It wants a lower-court order halting border wall construction in the Big Bend region of West Texas lifted.

US District Judge Kathleen Cardone, sitting in El Paso, issued the injunction on 2 October. She found the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in arguing that waivers of environmental and other laws exceeded the Homeland Security secretary's authority.

The lawsuit was brought by groups including the Center for Biological Diversity. Opponents say the remote area has historically low illegal crossings. The government says the sector is an area of high illegal entry, and that a 1996 law gives the secretary waiver powers.
Al Jazeera put the project's cost at $1.7bn, covering vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology. The Supreme Court had not responded at the time of reporting.

stories.stand: Justices refused to let the Bureau of Prisons end hormone therapy and surgeries for transgender prisoners while a legal challenge continues.
body: The US Supreme Court on Wednesday refused a Trump administration request to enforce new medical restrictions for transgender federal prisoners. The brief, unsigned order gave no reasons.
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas said they would have allowed the policy to take effect while the case continues.

The Bureau of Prisons policy, issued in February, would end surgeries and taper off hormone therapy for inmates with gender dysphoria. It would also end accommodations such as wigs and makeup. It followed an executive order from President Trump.
US District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the policy, and a divided appeals court panel left his order in place. The administration said the policy was needed to maintain institutional security.

body: The Electoral Commission has fined Reform UK for failing to show it was the publisher of campaign material. The original penalty was £1,750.
Reform missed the payment deadline and had to pay £2,187.50 instead, Left Foot Forward reported. It has since paid.
The Commission found three Reform social media accounts lacked digital imprints between at least November 2025 and January 2026. A Telegraph advert published in February 2026 also had no imprint.
The Commission said the advert aimed to secure success for Reform candidates in the May 2026 elections, so an imprint was required.

stories.head: Reform UK says it has reported ITV to police over undercover film
stories.say: Reform UK says it has reported ITV journalists to the police over an undercover documentary that showed party figures using racist language. ITV says it stands by its journalism.
stories.stand: The party is targeting journalists behind a documentary that showed councillors and candidates using racist language; ITV says it stands by its work.
body: Reform UK says it has reported several ITV journalists and the broadcaster's board to the police. The move follows an ITV Exposure documentary, Undercover: A Year In Reform, broadcast on Sunday 18 October.
The programme showed councillors and candidates in the party using racist language.

Zia Yusuf, Reform's home affairs spokesman, claimed an undercover reporter had doctored her passport to become a party press officer. He said Reform also plans civil proceedings. It is unclear which police force received the report.
ITV said it stands by its journalism and that the programme complied with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code. It said it would cooperate fully if police made contact.

stories.head: Cabinet split grows over Mahmood's plan for longer settlement wait
stories.say: Shabana Mahmood's plan to make migrants wait fifteen years for permanent residence has drawn criticism from cabinet colleagues Angela Rayner and Miatta Fahnbulleh.
stories.stand: Ministers Angela Rayner and Miatta Fahnbulleh have criticised the home secretary's plan to make migrants wait 15 years for permanent residence.
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood faces cabinet criticism over plans to extend the wait for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 15.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has publicly criticised the policy, which would apply retrospectively to people who arrived in 2021. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh wrote that longer waits threaten the process of building cohesion.
About 100 Labour MPs reportedly oppose the plans. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering exempting care workers, which the Home Office opposes, LBC reported.

Mahmood has said a majority of Labour MPs back the reforms. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested her party could vote with Labour to pass them. The plans could reach Parliament as soon as next month.

stories.head: Birmingham Lib Dem-Green coalition under pressure over Zionism motion
stories.say: Birmingham's Liberal Democrat council leader says his coalition with the Greens will continue, despite Ed Davey calling a Green conference motion on Zionism antisemitic.
stories.stand: Ed Davey wants Green partners to reject a conference motion he calls antisemitic, but Birmingham's Lib Dem council leader says the coalition will continue.
body: Birmingham City Council's ruling coalition is under pressure after the Green Party conference passed a motion declaring Zionism is racism. Critics call the motion antisemitic.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey called it deeply offensive and antisemitic. He urged Lib Dem council leaders to demand that Green partners publicly reject it.
Roger Harmer, the Lib Dem leader of the council, says he will not leave the coalition with Greens and independents. At least two Green councillors in Birmingham have publicly backed the motion.
Conservative councillor Meirion Jenkins says the Lib Dems cannot condemn the Greens nationally while working with them locally. The Green Party says it does not tolerate discrimination or harassment.

stories.head: Irish parliament votes to scrap UN mandate rule for peacekeeping
stories.say: Ireland's parliament has voted seventy-nine to seventy-one to scrap the requirement for a UN mandate before sending troops abroad on peacekeeping missions.
stories.stand: The Dáil backed abolishing the triple lock, removing the need for UN approval before Irish troops are sent on overseas missions.
body: Ireland's Dáil has voted 79 to 71 to abolish the triple lock on overseas military deployments. The vote came on Wednesday after a heated debate of about three and a half hours.
The triple lock requires a government decision, Dáil approval and a UN mandate to send more than 12 Defence Forces personnel abroad. The bill removes the UN requirement.
Defence Minister Helen McEntee said the system was not working, citing Security Council resistance. The government says permanent members such as Russia can veto missions.
Sinn Féin called the change risky and reckless, and wants a referendum. McEntee opposes holding one.

stories.head: Peru's Senate gives Keiko Fujimori 90 days to legislate on crime
stories.say: Peru's Senate has handed President Keiko Fujimori ninety days of powers to make anti-crime laws without Congress, including letting troops join the fight against gangs.
stories.stand: The president can now issue anti-crime laws without going through Congress, including allowing the armed forces to join the fight against gangs.
body: Peru's Senate on Wednesday approved a bill letting President Keiko Fujimori legislate against organised crime without going through Congress. The powers last 90 days.
They cover migration control, weapons use and prison reform. They also let her authorise the armed forces to join the fight against criminal gangs when police risk being overwhelmed.
The Chamber of Deputies had already approved the bill, but senators added new powers. The opposition fears soldiers could commit abuses.
Fujimori, who took office in July, campaigned on confronting crime. Peru is facing a sharp rise in homicides and extortion, El Tiempo reported.

stories.head: Milei calls Sánchez a dictator on Madrid visit before Spanish vote
stories.say: On a visit to Madrid, Argentina's Javier Milei called Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez a dictator and urged voters to oust the Socialists in next month's election.
stories.stand: Argentina's president urged Spaniards to vote out the Socialists ahead of the 29 November election; Spain's foreign ministry condemned his remarks.
body: Argentine President Javier Milei called Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez an unpresentable dictator at a breakfast event in Madrid on Wednesday. He urged Spaniards to kick the Socialists out.
The visit came ahead of Spain's snap general election on 29 November. Milei praised Vox leader Santiago Abascal and Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, whom he met later.
Spain's foreign ministry condemned the remarks as insults and said Spain does not accept outside interference, Infobae reported. Sánchez's Socialists hung a banner embracing the label leftists.
Milei held no meeting with Sánchez's government or with King Felipe VI. In 2024, Spain withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires after Milei's remarks about Sánchez's wife.

stories.say: Romania has a new government after parliament backed diplomat Luca Niculescu's minority cabinet by two hundred and eighty votes to fifty-eight on Tuesday.
stories.stand: Parliament backed the diplomat's cabinet by 280 votes to 58, ending a months-long political impasse.
body: Romania swore in a new cabinet led by Prime Minister Luca Niculescu on Tuesday. Parliament had backed it by 280 votes to 58.
Niculescu, 55, is an independent diplomat and former journalist. He leads a minority government, with support pledged by the Social Democrats among others.
President Nicușor Dan nominated him on 5 October, after three earlier nominees failed to form a government. Ilie Bolojan's government was ousted in a no-confidence vote in May.
Niculescu has put reducing a large budget deficit at the top of his agenda.

stories.head: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel prices surge
stories.say: Inflation in the UK climbed to three and a half per cent in September, driven by soaring fuel prices. City economists now expect the Bank of England to raise rates in November.
stories.stand: Consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, the highest in almost a year, putting pressure on the Bank of England to raise rates.
body: Consumer price inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. Prices rose 0.4% in the month.

Transport made the largest upward contribution. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier, and the average petrol price reached 169.5p a litre, the highest since August 2022. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%. Services inflation rose to 3.7% from 3.4%.

City AM reported that economists now expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates in November, about a week after John Healey's Budget. Bank Rate has stood at 3.75% since a cut at the end of 2025. Thomas Pugh of RSM said the data almost guaranteed a hike.

stories.head: UK borrowing of £24.5bn in September beats official forecast
stories.say: Government borrowing reached twenty-four and a half billion pounds in September, almost two billion more than forecast, as debt interest costs rose sharply on a year earlier.
stories.stand: Public sector borrowing was £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, with debt interest also above forecast, official figures show.
body: The UK public sector borrowed £24.5bn in September, £1.8bn more than a year earlier and £1.9bn above the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecast, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday.
Central government debt interest was £10.9bn in the month, up £1.6bn. Receipts rose 5.2% to £90.1bn, while spending rose 5.6% to £111.3bn.
Borrowing in the financial year to September totalled £97.8bn. That is £4.4bn less than a year earlier but £6.0bn above forecast. Public sector net debt was provisionally £3,005.0bn, or 94.0% of GDP.

stories.head: Tesla beats forecasts but car revenue falls and profit drops
stories.say: Tesla beat forecasts with revenue of just over twenty-eight billion dollars, but car revenue fell three per cent and net income fell to seven hundred and eighty-seven million.
stories.stand: Tesla's revenue and adjusted earnings beat forecasts, a day after Elon Musk floated combining it with SpaceX, but car revenue and net income fell.
body: Tesla reported third-quarter revenue of $28.05bn on Wednesday, slightly above the $27.9bn analysts expected. Adjusted earnings of 48 cents a share beat forecasts of 43 cents.
Automotive revenue fell 3% to $20.56bn, and deliveries were 486,532. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88bn, while services and other revenue rose 33% to $4.61bn. Net income fell to $787m.

Yahoo Finance reported that capital spending more than doubled to $3.73bn and free cash flow fell 62% to $1.53bn. The results came a day after Elon Musk said on a SpaceX call that combining the two companies would be a good idea.

stories.head: French 10-year borrowing costs top 5% for first time since 2002
stories.say: France's ten-year borrowing costs rose above five per cent on Wednesday for the first time in twenty-four years, amid budget deadlock and nationwide protests.
stories.stand: The yield on France's benchmark bond passed 5% as the government struggles to pass its 2027 budget and protests spread.
body: The yield on France's 10-year government bond rose above 5% on Wednesday, the first time in 24 years. Brit Brief reported that it rose more than 8 basis points in morning trading before easing to 4.99%.
Trading Economics put the gap over German 10-year Bunds at about 160 basis points, the widest since the eurozone debt crisis. Investors are also awaiting a Moody's credit rating review.

The rise follows political deadlock over the 2027 budget and weeks of protests. Authorities have imposed curfews in several cities. France's deficit was 5.1% of GDP in 2025, with debt at 115.6% of GDP.

stories.say: Elon Musk has pledged one SpaceX share for every child in America next year, a gift estimated at about ten point seven billion dollars, which Donald Trump linked to Trump Accounts.
stories.stand: Musk has not said who qualifies or how the shares would be delivered; Treasury rules let donors gift stock to children's Trump Accounts.
body: Elon Musk pledged on X on Monday to give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year. At SpaceX's closing price of $146.03 on 16 October, the gift to about 73 million under-18s would be worth about $10.7bn.
President Donald Trump thanked Musk and linked the gift to Trump Accounts, the child savings accounts created under his tax law. Musk has not said who qualifies or how the shares would be delivered.

Under Treasury rules in force since 30 September, donors can give company stock to the accounts. Families cannot refuse donated shares, which generally cannot be sold for five years or until the end of the year the child turns 17.

stories.say: Social security workers in Mexico marched through the capital on Wednesday, saying they would accept an eight per cent pay rise only if union leader Rafael Olivos steps down.
stories.stand: Staff at Mexico's social security institute also protested over shortages of staff, medicines and supplies, and plan more marches this month.
body: Workers at the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) marched through Mexico City on Wednesday over pay, supplies and their union leadership. The march partially blocked Paseo de la Reforma, according to Infobae.

IMSS director Zoé Robledo has announced an 8% salary increase. Dissident workers said they would accept it only if Rafael Olivos, secretary general of the SNTSS union, stepped down and an extraordinary national congress was called. Olivos has refused to call one.
Workers also complain of shortages of staff, medicines and supplies. Uno TV reported earlier that protesters had camped outside IMSS headquarters. Further protests are planned on 22 and 30 October.

stories.say: South Korea's central bank kept interest rates at three per cent on Thursday, pausing after two hikes to judge their effect before deciding on further increases.
stories.stand: All seven board members voted to hold, with the bank saying growth is set to beat its forecasts and inflation to stay above target.
body: The Bank of Korea kept its base rate at 3.00% on Thursday after raising it in July and August. All seven members of the Monetary Policy Board voted to hold.
The board said it would judge the timing and pace of further hikes after assessing the earlier increases. It cited uncertainty over the Middle East and major economies' policies.
Consumer inflation was 2.9% in September. The bank expects growth this year and next to exceed its August forecasts of 3.3% and 2.9%, helped by strong chip exports. Seoul house prices remain a risk.

stories.head: First New World screwworm case found in US wildlife
stories.say: A flesh-eating parasite has been found in American wildlife for the first time. The USDA says New World screwworm turned up in an elk on a Texas game ranch.
stories.stand: The USDA confirmed the parasite in an elk shot on a Texas game ranch, while New Mexico reported a separate case in a beef cow.
body: The US Department of Agriculture confirmed on Wednesday the first detection of New World screwworm in American wildlife. The case was an elk on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas, reported after a hunter shot it.
The USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department are expanding wildlife surveillance in the area. The Texas Animal Health Commission will change an existing infested zone.

Separately, the New Mexico Department of Agriculture said a case had been confirmed in a beef cow in Otero County. A minimum infested zone with a 20km radius has been set, and animals inside must be inspected before moving.

The fly lays eggs in open wounds of warm-blooded animals, and its larvae feed on living tissue. It was eradicated from the US decades ago but has spread north through Central America and Mexico. The USDA says it does not affect food safety.

stories.head: Ancient proteins tie Chinese Xujiayao fossils to Denisovans
stories.say: Proteins from fossil bones in northern China point to Denisovans. A Nature study says a telltale protein variant places the Xujiayao remains in that lineage.
stories.stand: A Nature study found a Denisovan-specific protein variant in Xujiayao fossils, and argues several East Asian skulls belong to the same lineage.
body: Researchers have linked hominin fossils from Xujiayao in northern China to the Denisovans, an extinct group of ancient humans. The study was published online in Nature on Wednesday.
The team analysed proteins from two specimens, a skull bone and part of a lower jaw. They identified 18 original proteins. One collagen protein carried a variant known only in Denisovans.

The remains come from layers dated to between about 199,000 and 138,000 years ago. Comparing shapes, the authors argue that fossils from Harbin, Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong also belong to the Denisovan lineage.
They describe Denisovans as having a low skull with near-parallel side walls and a massive brow ridge. The corresponding author is Qiaomei Fu of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

stories.head: Skeleton in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin likely an abbot
stories.say: A skeleton in a Roman stone coffin at Westminster Abbey was probably an Anglo-Saxon abbot. Radiocarbon dating puts the burial between 987 and 1052.
stories.stand: Radiocarbon dating shows the man buried in a reused fourth-century sarcophagus died around the 11th century, and the Abbey's archaeologist says he was almost certainly an abbot.
body: A skeleton in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey was probably an early abbot, according to a study by Warwick Rodwell, the Abbey's consultant archaeologist. It was published on Wednesday in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association.
Radiocarbon dating of the bones places the burial between 987 and 1052. The limestone coffin carries a fourth-century inscription to Valerius Amandinus, who the researchers say was not its occupant.
The skeleton is of a middle-aged man. Rodwell's leading candidate is Abbot Aelfwig, who died around 1020, with his successor Wulfnoth another possibility.
The burial had been looted before the sarcophagus was recovered in the 19th century. It is now on display in the Abbey's Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

stories.head: Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight into Thursday
stories.say: The Orionid meteor shower, made of dust from Halley's Comet, peaks overnight into Thursday. A bright moon will get in the way until it sets, so the hours before dawn are best.
stories.stand: Debris from Halley's Comet produces up to about 20 meteors an hour under dark skies, though a bright moon will hide many until it sets.
body: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight from Wednesday into Thursday. The meteors are debris from Halley's Comet burning up in Earth's atmosphere.
Under dark skies, viewers may see up to about 20 meteors an hour. The meteors are fast, hitting the atmosphere at about 66km per second.
A waxing gibbous moon will brighten much of the night. The best viewing is in the hours before dawn on Thursday, after the moon sets.
The meteors appear to come from the constellation Orion, near the red star Betelgeuse, but can be seen across the sky.

stories.stand: A developmental RS-25 engine ran for about 500 seconds at Stennis Space Center, testing flight parts and a new nozzle thermal protection system.
body: NASA test-fired a developmental RS-25 engine on Wednesday at Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. It ran for about 500 seconds, the same as during a Space Launch System launch.
The engine reached up to 111% power, the thrust level new production engines need to launch SLS and Orion. This engine will not fly.
The test was used to accept flight components for future Artemis missions and to validate a new thermal protection system for the nozzle. L3Harris Technologies is the prime contractor.

stories.stand: NASA said contract actions on the fission reactor and power conversion system will cut risk and keep the Mars demonstration on track for launch in late 2028.
body: NASA said on Tuesday it had agreed key contract actions to speed work on SR-1 Freedom, a fission-powered spacecraft bound for Mars. The agency says the steps reduce technical risk and keep the mission on course for launch in late 2028.
The spacecraft will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Its power module includes a fission reactor and a system that turns heat into electricity.

Sierra Lobo will provide the power conversion system at NASA's Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. The Department of Energy's Idaho National Laboratory is designing the reactor, which will stay inactive until the craft leaves Earth orbit.
The mission will also carry three Mars helicopters based on the Ingenuity design.

stories.head: Lost Schrödinger manuscript defends a deterministic quantum view
stories.say: An unpublished paper by Erwin Schrödinger has resurfaced after more than 80 years. In it he argued experiments could never prove the quantum world truly random, or not.
stories.stand: A physics historian has brought to light a three-page paper in which Schrödinger built a deterministic model that reproduces quantum probabilities.
body: A three-page manuscript by Erwin Schrödinger has come to light after more than 80 years in an Austrian archive. Physics historian Flavio Del Santo of the University of Geneva describes it in a preprint.
Schrödinger wrote it sometime after November 1944, in reply to Edmund Whittaker. Whittaker had argued in 1943 that quantum randomness rules out hidden variables.
Schrödinger built a model that reproduces quantum probabilities deterministically. He argued that evidence and logic could never prove either view impossible.
Why he never published it is unknown. Del Santo suggests he may have seen similar work by Heinrich Pelzer in 1944.

stories.head: Robotic metamaterial forms a time crystal from random vibrations
stories.say: Physicists have built a robotic material that settles into its own steady rhythm, a kind of time crystal. Random jiggles merge into one synchronised wave.
stories.stand: A Dutch-led team showed a mechatronic honeycomb lattice turns random vibrations into one stable, self-sustained rhythm that survives noise.
body: An international team led by Jonas Veenstra of the University of Amsterdam has built a mechanical metamaterial that behaves as a time crystal. The work is published in Nature.
The material is a honeycomb lattice of 37 units with sensors, actuators and small controllers. Each unit pushes its neighbours unequally, so one compresses while another expands.

After random nudges, fast vibrations of about 30 times a second gave way to larger, slower waves, until the whole structure moved in sync. The team says small random changes did not destroy this order.
Leiden University, a partner in the work, says the motion is driven by an internal energy source rather than an outside rhythm.

stories.head: Single molecules on a surface reach quantum coherence limit
stories.say: Physicists in Germany have kept single molecules on a crystal surface as quantum-coherent as nature allows, using an ultra-clean surface made in a vacuum.
stories.stand: A Max Planck team says molecules attached to a surface reached the Fourier limit of optical coherence for the first time, reported in Science.
body: Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light say individual molecules on a crystal surface have reached the Fourier limit. That is the longest their quantum optical coherence can physically last.
The institute says it is the first time this has been achieved for molecules attached to a surface. The work, led by Vahid Sandoghdar, is published in Science.
The team cleaned an organic crystal by slowly evaporating its top layers in a vacuum, then cooled it to a few degrees above absolute zero. They then deposited molecules onto the clean surface.
In noisy surroundings, coherence can vanish hundreds or thousands of times faster than this limit. The team plans to combine the method with microscopes that can steer single molecules.

stories.head: Uganda denies link to Nigeria's first Ebola case
stories.say: Uganda insists Nigeria's first Ebola patient was not infected there, saying it has no active cases. The woman, now isolated in Abuja, has the Bundibugyo strain behind Congo's outbreak.
stories.stand: Uganda says the Abuja patient only passed through the country, as Nigeria monitors 44 contacts of the woman with the Bundibugyo strain.
body: Uganda's health ministry has denied that Nigeria's first Ebola case was infected in Uganda. It said travel through the country does not establish that infection happened there, and that Uganda has no confirmed active cases.

The patient is a woman who arrived in Nigeria from Uganda. According to the WHO, she sought care at a private facility in Abuja on 11 October. Tests confirmed Ebola on 20 October. She is in isolation.

Nigerian authorities are monitoring 44 contacts, including health workers. The case is the Bundibugyo strain that is driving the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The WHO says Nigeria is the fifth country to detect it.

Africa CDC is convening crisis talks of African health ministers. Kenya has reported nine cases, all linked to one patient who travelled from Congo. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain.

stories.head: Diabetes and ADHD drugs tested on Alzheimer's patients in UK trial

stories.stand: The AD-SMART platform trial will test existing drugs at once and drop those that fail, with first results expected by 2030.
body: A UK trial called AD-SMART has begun testing whether existing drugs can help people with Alzheimer's disease. It starts with metformin, a type 2 diabetes drug, and atomoxetine, an ADHD medicine.

The trial tests several drugs at once. Drugs showing no benefit are dropped and new ones can be added. It is led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK, and the first drug results are expected by 2030.

The chief investigator is Prof Paresh Malhotra of Imperial College London. Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the launch and called finding dementia drugs a national priority. His father, Roy Burnham, died of dementia in September.

stories.stand: An Oxford study of blood from 2,555 men found proteins tied to later and aggressive prostate cancer, though it is not yet a usable test.
body: University of Oxford researchers have identified blood proteins linked to prostate cancer diagnosed years later. The study is published in European Urology.

The team measured more than 6,000 proteins in blood from 982 men who later developed prostate cancer and 1,573 randomly selected men. The samples came from the EPIC cohort, with about 16 years of follow-up.

An outside expert, Prof Prabhakar Rajan of Queen Mary University of London, said it does not yet show a protein blood test can reliably identify men at risk.

stories.head: FDA approves GSK's Hibsago, first antisense drug for chronic hepatitis B
stories.say: American regulators have approved GSK's Hibsago for chronic hepatitis B. In trials, about one in five patients kept the virus under control after stopping all treatment.
stories.stand: The weekly injection, given for 24 weeks alongside antivirals, let 24% of trial patients stop their existing medicine, against none on placebo.
body: The US Food and Drug Administration approved GSK's bepirovirsen, sold as Hibsago, for chronic hepatitis B on Tuesday 20 October. It is the first antisense drug approved for the disease.
It is for adults without cirrhosis whose virus is already suppressed by antivirals. Patients take a weekly injection for 24 weeks alongside their usual medicine.
In two phase 3 trials, 24% of patients on Hibsago met the criteria to stop their existing antiviral, against none on placebo. Functional cure rates were 20% and 19%.
The drug carries a boxed warning for serious liver reactions and low platelet counts, which can raise the risk of bleeding.

body: The Department of Health and Social Care says it has met its target to speed up the set-up of clinical trials, with delivery times cut by 35%.

stories.say: Poland's lower house has voted to allow abortion again for severe foetal abnormalities. The bills still need the Senate and President Karol Nawrocki, who has opposed easing restrictions.
stories.stand: The Sejm passed two narrow bills on Tuesday; even if enacted, Poland and Malta would remain the only EU states without abortion on request.
body: Poland's lower house, the Sejm, passed two abortion bills on Tuesday 20 October. One would again allow abortion for severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities. It passed by 233 votes to 203.
The other would exempt doctors, nurses and midwives from criminal liability when an abortion is medically necessary. It passed by 217 votes to 213.

The bills need Senate approval and the signature of President Karol Nawrocki, who has said he would not support easing restrictions. The governing coalition lacks the three-fifths majority needed to override a veto.
Even if enacted, Poland and Malta would remain the only EU countries without legal abortion on request in early pregnancy.

Researchers followed 461,682 Americans aged 50 to 71 in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, for a median of 18.8 years.

The authors note the study is observational, diet was recorded only once, and most participants were older white Americans.

stories.say: Ministers have approved the Jackdaw gas field off Aberdeen, with first gas expected within weeks. Andy Burnham says it protects jobs; the Greens call it climate vandalism.
body: The UK government has approved production at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, off Aberdeen. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh agreed on Wednesday that the North Sea Transition Authority could grant consent.

Owner Adura, a joint venture of Shell and Equinor, says the field could heat about 1.4 million homes at peak. The government expects it to lift domestic gas production by about 6%. First gas could flow by the end of October.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the decision would protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm. He said it would not hinder renewable energy targets. According to Al Jazeera, Fahnbulleh told LBC it would not mean cheaper bills.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski called it climate vandalism, and Greenpeace UK also criticised it. The original 2022 consent was quashed by a Scottish court over unassessed emissions from burning the gas. A decision on the Rosebank oil field will take longer.

stories.say: The UN's environment agency says limiting warming to 1.5C without overshoot is now out of reach. Current policies point to about 2.8C by the end of the century.
body: The UN Environment Programme says the chance of keeping global warming below 1.5C with no or limited overshoot is gone. Its Emissions Gap Report 2026 was published on Wednesday.
The report says current policies point to about 2.8C of warming by 2100, according to Carbon Brief. Global emissions were 58.4 gigatonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2025, similar to 2024.
To keep overshoot as small as possible, emissions must fall 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035 from 2025 levels. Fully delivered national pledges would cut them only 11-15% by 2035.
Carbon Brief reports that the US exit from the Paris Agreement raised projected 2035 emissions by about 3 gigatonnes. G20 members account for 76% of global emissions.

stories.say: Fire hotspots in Brazil's Amazon rose by sixty-two per cent in the first half of October, even as deforestation fell to its lowest level since 1988.
body: Satellites detected 9,045 fire hotspots in Brazil's Amazon in the first half of October, 62% more than a year earlier, MercoPress reported. A drought worsened by El Niño has dried the forest.
Deforestation fell 42% to 3,355 sq km between August 2025 and July 2026, the lowest since 1988. The federal government has deployed more than 300 firefighters and 11 aircraft.

Ane Alencar of the Amazon Environmental Research Institute said most fires are set deliberately, generally to clear land for cattle. She noted the rise began after the 4 October first round of the presidential election.
Jair Schmitt, head of the environment agency Ibama, said police and intelligence services are investigating whether the fires were orchestrated.

stories.head: Scientists alarmed by southern right whale die-off in Argentina
stories.stand: Unofficial reports cite more than 300 dead whales around Península Valdés this season, which scientists expect could be the worst on record.
stories.say: Scientists in Argentina are investigating an unusual die-off of southern right whales, with unofficial reports citing more than three hundred dead at Península Valdés.
body: Scientists in Argentina are investigating an unusual die-off of southern right whales around Península Valdés in Chubut province. Unofficial reports cite more than 300 dead whales, MercoPress reported.
No official toll will be released until the season ends. The previous record in the monitoring programme was 113 dead calves in 2012.

Calf deaths have been linked to bacteria that may enter through wounds, such as those made by kelp gulls. For adults, a toxic algal bloom known as red tide is suspected. Researchers say warming seas linked to climate change or El Niño may play a role.
Marcela Uhart of the University of California, Davis leads the health monitoring programme. This season, 1,375 whales were recorded, including 409 calves.

stories.head: Tunisia sentences 10 activists over Gabes anti-pollution protest
stories.stand: Two received one-year jail terms and eight suspended sentences over a 2020 protest against a state-run phosphate plant, their lawyer said.
stories.say: A Tunisian court has sentenced ten activists over a 2020 protest against pollution from a phosphate plant in Gabes. Two were given one-year jail terms, their lawyer said.
body: A Tunisian court has sentenced 10 environmental activists over a 2020 protest against pollution from a phosphate plant in Gabes. Defence lawyer Hamida Chaieb said two received one-year jail terms and eight six-month suspended sentences.

The state-run factory brought the case, accusing the protesters of obstructing its operations. The activists believed the case had been dropped, but learned they had been sentenced in absentia in 2023. That led to a retrial.

Researchers have reported that some of the plant's waste and gases are radioactive. Tunisia aims to more than quadruple phosphate output by 2030, and a court rejected calls to suspend the plant in February.

stories.head: Valencia approves €23.5m flood aid after Storm Adam kills five
stories.stand: Up to €6,000 is on offer for damaged main homes after torrential rain in eastern Spain, as Pedro Sánchez visited worst-hit Oliva.
stories.say: Storm Adam has killed at least five people in eastern Spain, and the Valencian government has approved a twenty-three and a half million euro aid package.
body: Storm Adam has killed at least five people in eastern Spain, according to Euronews and the Olive Press. The Valencia region was worst hit, with the resort of Oliva at the centre.
Oliva recorded 600 litres of rain per square metre in 24 hours, Euronews reported. The Civil Guard evacuated more than 2,100 people and rescued almost 500 in the Valencia region.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited Oliva on Tuesday and pledged national resources for reconstruction. The Valencian government approved a €23.5m aid package, with up to €6,000 for damage to a main home.
AEMET, the state weather agency, kept warnings in nine provinces on Tuesday as heavy rain moved to Catalonia and the Balearics.

stories.head: UK launches taskforce on climate and nature security risks
stories.stand: Climate minister Katie White chaired the first meeting of a 16-member expert group on how climate change and nature loss threaten UK security.
stories.say: The government has set up a taskforce to examine how climate change and nature loss threaten UK security. Climate minister Katie White chaired its first meeting.
body: The government has set up a taskforce on the security risks of climate change and nature loss. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero announced it on Wednesday and described it as a world first.

Katie White, the Minister for Climate Transition, chaired the first meeting with Baroness Fiona Twycross. The 16 members include experts from the Bank of England, Chatham House, the National Trust and the International Crisis Group.

The group will identify and prioritise the biggest risks to UK security and resilience, and review government work on them. It will meet up to two times in 2026. The government said summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record.

stories.head: Gas behind nearly 90% of rise in UK electricity bills, analysis finds
stories.stand: Nesta analysis for Carbon Brief says wholesale costs drove £161 of a £180 real-terms rise in typical electricity bills since 2020.
stories.say: Wholesale gas costs explain nearly ninety per cent of the rise in UK electricity bills since 2020, according to analysis by the think tank Nesta.
body: Wholesale gas costs account for nearly 90% of the rise in UK household electricity bills since 2020, according to analysis by the think tank Nesta for Carbon Brief.
A typical electricity bill has risen £180 in real terms, of which £161 comes from wholesale costs. Dual-fuel bills rose 47% in real terms, from £1,175 in October 2020 to £1,723 in October 2026.

The analysis uses Ofgem price cap figures adjusted for inflation. It says renewable contracts for difference are cutting electricity bills by £17. Nesta's Andrew Sissons said rising gas prices, not net zero, have driven most of the increase.
UK wholesale gas was 220p a therm on 19 October, above the 2022 average, amid conflict in the Middle East.

stories.head: Toledo chemical leak forces evacuations as 50,000 told to shelter
stories.stand: A ruptured tank leaked in an industrial area of Toledo, Ohio, and officials let the chemical vent rather than send crews close to it.
stories.say: A ruptured chemical tank in Toledo, Ohio, forced evacuations, and more than fifty thousand people were told to stay indoors. Officials let the chemical vent.
body: A ruptured chemical tank leaked in an industrial area of Toledo, Ohio, on Tuesday night. Residents within a 1-mile radius were told to evacuate, and those within 3 miles to shelter in place.

WISN reported that more than 50,000 people were advised to shelter, with the zone reaching into Michigan. It named the chemical as glycidyl methacrylate, used in plastics and paints. The Ohio EPA said the leak followed an error during a material transfer.

City leaders let the chemical vent rather than send crews near the tank, fearing it could explode. ProMedica evaluated about 30 people for possible symptoms, and most were released. Toledo schools closed on Wednesday.

stories.head: AI-found PHP flaws knock government websites offline worldwide
stories.say: Websites from the Netherlands to Australia went dark as a precaution on Wednesday, after two critical flaws in the PHP web language, found with help from AI, were disclosed and patched.
stories.stand: Governments took sites offline as a precaution after two critical flaws in the PHP web language, found with AI tools, were disclosed and patched.
body: Governments in several countries took websites offline as a precaution on Wednesday after two critical flaws were disclosed in PHP, a language used by most websites. The flaws let attackers run their own code on servers without logging in.

PHP's developers released fixes and urged operators to update immediately. In the Netherlands, the national cyber security centre and the Overheid.nl government portal went offline. Services were also paused in Denmark, Finland and France, according to Daily Maverick and MercoPress.
Two security firms, Calif and Wiz, said they used AI models to find the flaws. Amazon said it saw exploitation attempts from 17 October, before public disclosure.
In Australia, the Signals Directorate issued a rare critical alert, ABC News reported. GovCMS, which hosts many government websites, blocked direct server access but kept cached pages online.

stories.head: Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn over Facebook privacy claims
stories.say: A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay twenty-five billion dollars after a jury found it misled Facebook users about their data. Meta says it expects to win on appeal.
stories.stand: A New Mexico judge set a $25bn penalty after a jury found Meta misled users about how it handled their data, in a case rooted in Cambridge Analytica.
body: A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found it misled Facebook users about how it handled their personal data. Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday.
The case grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which Facebook data was harvested for political ads around the 2016 US election. The jury reached its verdict in September.

The state had sought $35bn to $40bn. Meta had argued that any award above about $3.4bn would violate due process. Its chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the company was confident of winning on appeal.
Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the ruling sent a clear message to Silicon Valley. The money is due to go towards education in the state, but may not arrive for years.

stories.head: Meta sued in Australian class action over harm to children
stories.say: Eight people who say Facebook and Instagram harmed them as children are suing Meta in Australia's Federal Court, alleging its algorithms fostered addiction. Meta says it will fight it.
stories.stand: Eight people who say Facebook and Instagram harmed them as children have filed a class action against Meta in Australia's Federal Court.
body: A class action has been filed against Meta in the Federal Court of Australia, alleging Facebook and Instagram harmed children. Law firm MinterEllison brought the case on behalf of eight plaintiffs.
They say they were harmed while under 18 and are seeking compensation. The suit alleges the platforms exposed children to damaging material and used algorithms to foster addiction.
Meta said it was aware of the claim and would defend itself vigorously. The court has barred reporting that could identify the applicants, as well as the statement of claim.

The case could be the first in Australia to blame social media for harming users. Australia already bans social media for under-16s. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle claims from nearly all US states.

stories.head: US lawmakers call for inquiry into Starlink slowdown that hit Ukraine
stories.say: Lawmakers in Washington want to know who ordered the Starlink slowdown that Ukraine says brought down its interceptor drones. Donald Trump says he was not involved.
stories.stand: Lawmakers from both parties want to know who ordered a Starlink speed cap that Ukraine says disrupted its drones. Donald Trump denies involvement.
body: US lawmakers from both parties have called for an investigation into who ordered a slowdown of Starlink satellite internet used by Ukraine's military. The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk ordered the speed cap.

Republican congressman Brian Fitzpatrick said Musk and others may need to testify under oath, Stars and Stripes reported. Democrats Rosa DeLauro and Betty McCollum asked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to investigate and report within 30 days.
Donald Trump said on Wednesday he was not involved, according to Political Wire, citing CNBC. Musk has said speed limits are set by the US military and ultimately the president.
Volodymyr Zelensky says the cap made terminals shut down at high speeds, causing interceptor drones to crash. He said on Wednesday that access was still limited.

stories.head: OpenAI's GPT-6 models come to Google Cloud
stories.say: OpenAI's newest GPT-6 models are coming to Google Cloud, which means a rival's flagship AI now runs on all three of America's biggest cloud platforms.
stories.stand: Google Cloud will offer OpenAI's GPT-6 models to business customers, putting OpenAI's models on all three major US cloud platforms.
body: Google Cloud will offer OpenAI's latest GPT-6 models to business customers, the companies announced on Wednesday. The Astra, Sol and Luna models will sit in Google's Model Garden.

The models are in private preview for selected enterprise customers, with wider availability expected in the coming weeks, according to Android Headlines. Developers can also connect OpenAI's Codex coding tools to Google's platform.

OpenAI's models were first exclusive to Microsoft's Azure and later came to Amazon Web Services. Google Cloud now offers models from OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude and its own Gemini. Google says customer prompts and outputs will not be used to train models.

stories.say: Apple has been ordered to open iPhones in Australia to rival app stores from March 2027, after losing to Epic Games. Fortnite returns to the App Store on Thursday.
stories.stand: A Federal Court judge ruled in Epic Games' case that Apple must allow third-party app stores in Australia from March 2027. Fortnite returns to the App Store.
body: An Australian court has ordered Apple to open its iPhone software to rival app stores, in a case brought by Epic Games. Federal Court Justice Jonathan Beach ruled on Wednesday, after a 2025 finding that Apple broke competition law.

From 1 March 2027, users with Australian Apple accounts must be able to install apps from third-party stores and websites, 9to5Mac reported. Apple must also allow alternative payment methods and external payment links.
Epic said Fortnite would return to the App Store in Australia on Thursday. Apple said it disagreed with many of the findings and would request a stay and appeal.

body: Most X posts spreading false claims about the US midterm elections carried no Community Note, according to an analysis by NewsGuard. The midterms are on 3 November.
NewsGuard found 189 posts advancing 27 false claims it had identified. Of those, 176, or 93.1%, had no note as of 20 October. Only 13 carried one.
Elon Musk posted four of the false claims, none with a note. X's press team did not respond to NewsGuard's request for comment.

body: China has said it opposes US sanctions on five Chinese companies linked to Linwei Ding, a former Google engineer. The US State Department imposed the sanctions on Monday.

body: Xbox is letting players pay by the hour to stream games through its cloud service, without a Game Pass subscription. The option, called Xbox Cloud Playtime, began testing with Xbox Insiders on Wednesday.
Packs cost $3.99 for 10 hours, $7.99 for 25 hours and $11.99 for 50 hours. That works out at between 24 and 40 cents an hour. The paid packs are ad-free and stream at the highest available quality.
A wider rollout is expected in November, Kotaku reported. It said Xbox was also moving towards an ad-supported tier.

body: The European Commission has opened a formal investigation into whether Booking.com breached the EU's Digital Services Act. It announced the probe on Wednesday.

body: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport announced the list on 22 October.
The four were chosen from nine longlisted bids by an expert advisory panel chaired by Sir Phil Redmond. Inverness-Highland, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon did not go through.
Each shortlisted place will receive at least £125,000 to develop its bid. The winner gets a £10 million prize fund and will be announced in early 2027.

body: The Canadian publisher Les Editions du Boreal has ended its relationship with Haitian-Canadian novelist Thelyson Orelien. It says artificial intelligence was used in writing his debut novel, C'etait ca ou mourir.

Boreal said an outside analysis of working drafts found traces of AI tags in some documents' metadata. It said it may never know how extensively AI was used. It will not reprint the novel or publish his future books.
A week earlier the publisher had backed the author. Al Jazeera reports that France's Goncourt prize had already removed the book from its shortlist after an AI detector flagged it.
Orelien has denied the allegations. Al Jazeera says he told Liberation on Wednesday he had used AI for historical research.

stories.head: Colombia to review more museums after National Museum removals
stories.stand: Protests continue in Bogota after President Abelardo de la Espriella's government took down about 30 works on social movements and political violence.
stories.say: Colombia's culture minister says more museums will have exhibitions redesigned, after works on feminism, LGBTQ rights and the peace deal were pulled from Bogota's National Museum.
body: Colombia's government has removed about 30 works from the National Museum in Bogota. They deal with feminist and LGBTQ+ movements, victims of political violence and the 2016 peace accord.

President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered the removals. He has said cultural spaces must not be taken over by "atheist social communism". Culture Minister Paola Holguin said the museum should not be used for political indoctrination.

On Monday a Bogota judge ordered the government to keep the removed works safe and not destroy, move or alter them, according to AFP. Holguin has since said other museums under her ministry are being reviewed.
Protests have been held outside the museum since 17 October. Al Jazeera reports that dozens demonstrated on Wednesday as riot police guarded the entrance.

stories.stand: The second-half spot kick in Seville gave Betis a third straight Champions League win and handed Feyenoord an eighth successive European away defeat.
stories.say: An Isco penalty gave Real Betis a one-nil win over Feyenoord in Seville on Wednesday, a third straight Champions League win, and Feyenoord's eighth European away defeat in a row.
body: Real Betis beat Feyenoord 1-0 at the Estadio La Cartuja in Seville in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Isco scored from the penalty spot in the 59th minute, according to NL Times, after a shot struck the arm of Jeremiah St. Juste.
It was Betis's third win from three games in the league phase. RTÉ reports they earlier beat Lille and Porto, both 3-2.
NL Times says it was Feyenoord's eighth consecutive away defeat in European competition, leaving them 26th of 36 teams.

stories.head: Arsenal concerned over Saka thigh injury after early exit at Bayern
stories.stand: Mikel Arteta said the injury does not look good; Bukayo Saka will have scans in London after leaving the field early in Munich.
stories.say: Arsenal are waiting on scans for Bukayo Saka, who went off early at Bayern Munich on Wednesday holding his thigh. Mikel Arteta said the medical staff were a bit concerned.
body: Bukayo Saka left the field early in Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich on Wednesday, holding his thigh. He was replaced by Eberechi Eze.
Goal reports that Saka pulled up without a challenge while making a routine pass, and will have further scans in London.
Mikel Arteta said the medical staff were a bit concerned and that it did not look good, but that they would have to wait and see.
Al Jazeera notes Saka is Arsenal's joint-top scorer this season. Arsenal play in the Premier League this weekend.

stories.head: Australia follow on and trail by 170 after Jansen takes five in Gqeberha
stories.stand: Australia were bowled out for 99 on day four of the second Test; Travis Head's unbeaten 87 took them to 156 for four at the close.
stories.say: Australia were bowled out for ninety-nine and made to follow on in Gqeberha. At stumps on day four they trailed by a hundred and seventy, with Travis Head on eighty-seven.
body: Australia were bowled out for 99 in reply to South Africa's 425 for nine declared on day four of the second Test at St George's Park, Gqeberha.
Marco Jansen took 5-33. South Africa enforced the follow-on, a lead of 326.
In their second innings Australia reached 156 for four at the close, still 170 behind. Travis Head was 87 not out, with Steve Smith, Marnus Labuschagne and Alex Carey among those out.
ABC News reports that Smith, who was off the field with a sore neck, is expected to bat again on day five. The match is the second of three Tests.

stories.head: James Anderson, 44, not offered new Lancashire contract
stories.stand: England's record Test wicket-taker is reported to be set to retire after Lancashire decided not to renew his deal for 2027.
stories.say: Lancashire have decided not to offer James Anderson a new contract, reports said on Wednesday. England's record Test wicket-taker, now forty-four, is said to be set to retire.
body: Lancashire have decided not to offer James Anderson a contract for 2027, according to reports first published by The Times on Wednesday. The club has declined to comment.
Reports say the 44-year-old is set to retire rather than join another county. He has played county cricket only for Lancashire.
Anderson is England's leading Test wicket-taker with 704 wickets. He captained Lancashire in 2026 and took 50 County Championship wickets as the club finished second from bottom of Division Two.
Paul Farbrace has joined as director of cricket and Richard Kenyon is the new chief executive.

stories.head: F1 race distance to return to 305km in 2028 after one-year cut
stories.stand: New FIA regulations shorten grands prix to about 290km in 2027, then restore the standard distance a year later.
stories.say: Formula One races will be cut to about two hundred and ninety kilometres in 2027, before returning to the standard three hundred and five kilometres in 2028, under new FIA rules.
body: Formula One's standard race distance will return to 305km in 2028, according to the FIA's newly published 2027 regulations.
For 2027 only, grands prix will be cut to about 290km. Monaco stays at 260km.
RacingNews365 reports the cut is linked to a shift in the engines' combustion-electric power split towards about 60/40, which means more fuel is burned per race.
A shorter race avoids larger fuel tanks and chassis changes for 2027, the outlet says.
